analysis.one_liner: Repeals a set of tax breaks for large oil and gas companies and puts the money into a clean-energy fund.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors and no committee action: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2007 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended roughly a dozen federal tax breaks enjoyed by the oil and gas industry — things like faster write-offs for drilling and refining equipment, a percentage depletion allowance, credits for enhanced oil recovery and marginal wells, and a deduction for domestic oil and gas production. The biggest provisions targeted 'large integrated oil companies' producing at least 500,000 barrels a day. All the money raised would have gone into a new Energy Trust Fund for renewable energy, efficiency, and conservation [S2; S3]. The bill was introduced by Senator Schumer in February 2007 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it [S1; S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been the public through the new Energy Trust Fund, which every dollar of the repealed tax breaks would fund for renewable energy, alternative fuels, efficiency, conservation, and clean-energy research [S3 sec. 201]. Taxpayers generally would have gained revenue that currently reduces what others owe. Renewable energy companies and researchers would have gained a dedicated funding stream. The bill is written so small oil and gas producers keep their existing breaks — the deepest cuts apply only to companies producing 500,000 or more barrels a day with over $1 billion in receipts [S3 secs. 110-112].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renewable energy and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Repeals a series of oil and gas tax preferences, including the intangible drilling cost deduction, the enhanced oil recovery credit, the marginal well credit, expedited depreciation of refining equipment and gas pipelines, and the domestic production deduction for large integrated oil companies [S2; S3 secs. 103-110].

Every dollar of revenue raised by the repeal is directed into a new Energy Trust Fund dedicated to clean renewable energy, alternative fuels, energy efficiency and conservation, and clean-energy research [S3 sec. 201].

The largest provisions are aimed specifically at 'large integrated oil companies' producing at least 500,000 barrels a day with over $1 billion in gross receipts, so the tax increase targets the biggest firms rather than small producers [S3 secs. 110-112].

analysis.who_pays: Large integrated oil companies — defined as producing at least 500,000 barrels a day with over $1 billion in gross receipts — would have paid billions more in taxes through the loss of drilling deductions, depletion allowances, refining and pipeline depreciation rules, production and foreign tax credit benefits, and a one-time inventory revaluation [S3 secs. 110-112]. Natural gas distribution and pipeline operators and refiners would have lost favorable depreciation treatment on new equipment [S3 secs. 103-105, 109]. Some portion of higher industry taxes could be passed to consumers through fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher taxes on oil and gas production, refining, and pipeline investment could be passed to consumers in the form of higher prices at the pump and for home heating, since the bill included no mechanism to prevent cost pass-through.

The bill's required LIFO inventory revaluation [S3 sec. 111] was a one-time, retroactive-style tax charge for the 2006 tax year on top of the forward-looking repeal of breaks, which critics would describe as singling out one industry for an extra assessment.

The bill attracted no cosponsors and no committee action, so even supporters in the Senate gave it no visible backing, raising the question of whether the proposal was designed to make a point rather than to move through the legislative process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real but indirect: ending roughly a dozen oil and gas tax preferences and routing the money into renewable energy and efficiency would have shifted billions in tax treatment from large oil companies toward public energy investment, with no direct cost to any taxpayer outside the industry. The main drawbacks are practical: energy companies might pass some of the tax increase to consumers through fuel prices, the LIFO revaluation was a one-time retroactive charge that opponents would call punitive, and the bill offered no protection against that price pass-through. On balance, the proposal would have cost the industry much more than it cost the public, but it also drew no cosponsors and was never refined through committee work, so its design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Schumer introduced the bill on February 16, 2007; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1; S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two-year Congress [S4].
The committee took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and all bills not enacted die at the end of a Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies kept all of the tax breaks the bill targeted — the drilling cost deduction, depletion allowance, refining and pipeline depreciation rules, domestic production deduction, and favorable foreign tax credit treatment — and no revenue was redirected to the Energy Trust Fund for clean energy. Because the bill never advanced, none of its provisions ever took effect.

for.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited no cosponsors; no further action is recorded.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (chaired by Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote appear in the record for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Integrated oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Fiercely defended the oil and gas tax provisions at issue in 2007 congressional debates over energy taxes; none of those provisions was repealed through this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so there is no record showing how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions strip away the intangible drilling cost deduction, depletion beyond basis, the enhanced oil recovery and marginal well credits, expedited depreciation of refining equipment, the Section 199 domestic production deduction, favorable foreign tax credit treatment, and impose a one-time LIFO inventory revaluation. Ordinary people would have gained cleaner-energy funding and revenue that currently stays with these companies.

The bill ends accelerated depreciation for natural gas distribution lines and Alaska natural gas pipelines and reclassifies gathering lines as 15-year property, modestly raising the cost of pipeline investment. These are narrower provisions that apply to infrastructure used to deliver energy to households.

The Energy Trust Fund would fund deployment of renewable energy, alternative fuels, energy efficiency, and related research, creating demand for clean-energy firms and technologies. This benefit runs alongside the public's interest in cheaper, cleaner energy.
